result: The study demonstrates that fractal cycles derived from EEG spectral slopes show cyclical fluctuations (4-6 times per night) with an average duration of ~89 minutes, closely matching classical sleep cycles (~90 minutes). Fractal and classical cycle durations correlated positively (r=0.5, p<0.001), and 81% of fractal cycles could be matched to classical cycles defined by hypnogram.
evaluation: All three reviewers affirm the core finding. The editor states the method is 'supported by solid evidence and analyses.' Reviewer 1 notes 'the manuscript amply illustrates through examples the strong overlap between fractal and classical cycle identification' and confirms 'a high percentage (81%) can be matched one-to-one between methods and sleep cycle duration is well correlated (around R = 0.5).' Reviewer 2 acknowledges 'results are fairly consistent between this and conventional sleep scoring.'

result: Children and adolescents showed shorter fractal cycles compared to young adults (76±34 vs 94±32 min, p<0.001, Cohen's d=-0.57), with fractal cycles showing higher sensitivity to age differences than classical cycles based on F-values, adjusted R squared, and effect sizes.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly states that 'the methods track certain global changes in sleep structure in different populations: shorter cycles in children.' The finding is presented as one of the key demonstrations of the method's validity across populations, and no reviewer challenges this result.

result: Medicated patients with depression showed longer fractal cycles compared to their unmedicated state (107±51 vs 92±38 min) and age-matched controls (104±49 vs 88±31 min). Patients taking REM-suppressive antidepressants showed longer cycles than those on REM-non-suppressive medications. Unmedicated patients showed comparable cycle durations to controls but had smaller amplitude of fractal descent in first cycles.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly confirms this finding, stating 'the methods track certain global changes in sleep structure in different populations: ... longer cycles in patients medicated with REM-suppressing anti-depressants.' No reviewer questions or challenges these depression-related findings, treating them as valid demonstrations of the method's clinical utility.

result: The fractal cycle algorithm detected cycles with skipped REM sleep in 91-98% of cases identified by human scorers, with inter-rater agreement between two human scorers at 91%. The algorithm's detection is based on identifying local peaks in fractal slope time series that correspond to 'lightening' of sleep in skipped cycles.
evaluation: No reviewer challenges the skipped cycle detection results. The high detection rate (91-98%) is presented as evidence of the algorithm's validity, and reviewers accept the overall performance of the method. The finding is treated as supporting evidence for the fractal cycle approach.

result: In adults, fractal cycle duration negatively correlated with age (r=-0.19, p=0.006), remaining significant after controlling for wakefulness (r=-0.18, p=0.011) and REM latency (r=-0.16, p=0.025). Classical cycles showed no correlation with age. The authors conclude fractal cycles are more sensitive to age-related alterations than classical cycles.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly notes this as a key difference between methods: 'The match between fractal and classical cycles is not one-to-one. For example, the fractal method identifies a correlation between age and cycle duration in adults that is not apparent with the classical method.' This is presented as an advantage of the fractal method, not a criticism.

result: Longer REM episodes and higher wakefulness after sleep onset (WASO) were associated with greater discrepancies between classical and fractal cycle durations. Shallower fractal descents were also associated with higher mismatch between the two cycle types.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 acknowledges that 'the difference between the fractal and classical methods appear to be linked to the uncertain definition of sleep cycles since they are tied to when exactly the cycle begins/ends and whether or not to count cycles during fractured sleep architecture.' This contextualizes the discrepancies as related to methodological differences rather than errors, implicitly accepting these findings.

result: Fractal cycles are specific to sleep and not observed during wake. Cycle-to-cycle dynamics showed an inverted U-shape for cycle durations and gradual decrease in amplitudes of fractal descents/ascents from early to late cycles. Fractal slopes show cycling nature over the entire night's sleep, unlike slow-wave activity which only cycles during the first part of the night.
evaluation: These overnight dynamics findings are not challenged by any reviewer. Reviewer 2 notes that 'from the fractal cycle perspective, waking and REM sleep are not very dissimilar,' which acknowledges the distinction between wake and sleep cycles. The characterization of fractal cycles as spanning the whole night is implicitly accepted.

result: Automatically identified classical sleep cycles only moderately correlated with those detected by human raters (r=0.3-0.7). The correlation between fractal and classical cycles (r=0.41-0.55, moderate) falls between automatic-manual classical cycle correlation and the strong correlation between two human scorers (r=0.7-0.9).
evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly notes that 'the discrepancies between the two are on the order of that found between classical cycles defined manually or via an automatic algorithm.' This contextualizes the moderate correlation as acceptable given the inherent variability in sleep cycle definition, effectively supporting the finding.

result: The authors conclude that fractal cycles are an objective, quantifiable, continuous and biologically plausible way to display sleep neural activity and its cycles, meaningfully adding to conventionally used hypnograms. They propose fractal cycles as a promising research tool relevant in health and disease that should be extensively studied.
evaluation: The editor calls this a 'valuable study' with a 'novel method' supported by 'solid evidence.' Reviewer 1 states 'the fractal cycle is an attractive method to study sleep architecture since it dispenses with time-consuming and potentially subjective manual identification' and notes it 'has the potential to be applied on animal studies.' Reviewer 2 affirms 'the main novelty of the study' and that 'the method appears to work well.' However, Reviewer 1 cautions 'it is unlikely that fractal scoring will be able to replace classical scoring directly,' suggesting complementary rather than replacement use.

result: Both REM- and wake-related smoothed fractal slopes could be defined as local peaks, which may explain some mismatches between fractal and classical cycle identification.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly notes 'from the fractal cycle perspective, waking and REM sleep are not very dissimilar. Combining these states underlies some of the key results of this study.' This directly acknowledges and accepts the observation that both states produce similar fractal slope patterns (peaks).
